<!-- https://medianville.netlify.app/agents/districts/dunmore.md -->

# D5 Rural town: Main Street, Dunmore

**Composite**: an invented block drawn from documented US patterns, not a real place. Part of https://medianville.netlify.app/agents/districts.md, which explains the layers and the ids.

Block id `dunmore`, on Main St. A grain-and-rail town that lost its railroad, its bank and its grocery; the mobile home park was sold to an investor in 2019.

The simulator puts 380 of the district's households on this block (`block_id = dunmore` in households.csv and records.csv).

## Across the whole district (the district tier)

**Economic** (changes over years)

- **DW1** · 2023 · Cash where the banks left. Across the rural towns, banking means a drive or a fee. About two-thirds of unbanked households use only cash, and an out-of-network ATM withdrawal averages a record $4.86.
  - Types: economic, social. Evidence: E011, E014.
- **DW2** · 2016 · Home care hours go unfilled. Approved home care often goes unstaffed. In one agency survey, 85% lacked staff to cover every shift and 43% left shifts unfilled at least seven times a month; one rural state counted about 11,000 approved hours unstaffed each week.
  - Types: economic, social. Rests on: DH1, Fewer, bigger farms. Evidence: E053, E054, E055.
- **DW3** · 2024 · Called in on a day off. The town's jobs are thin and the stores are short-staffed. Workers describe being called in at the last minute, even on days off, and scrambling for child care when they are.
  - Types: economic. Evidence: E040, E047.

**Political** (changes over decades)

- **DW4** · 2026 · Dialysis an hour away. Rural residents average about 14 miles to the nearest dialysis unit, but closures stretch that fast: when one small hospital closed its unit, a patient's time on the road tripled to more than nine hours a week.
  - Types: political, environmental. Rests on: DH1, Fewer, bigger farms. Evidence: E051, E052.

**Built & natural** (changes over generations)

- **DE1** · ongoing · Homes on rented land. Manufactured homes are far more common in rural towns than in cities. Many sit on rented lots in parks, so the owners own the house but not the ground under it, and moving the house is rarely practical.
  - Types: environmental, social. Rests on: DH1, Fewer, bigger farms. Source: Census American Community Survey (housing type), with the Housing Assistance Council's rural tabulations; CFPB, Manufactured Housing Finance (2021).

**Historical** (bedrock, lasts a century)

- **DH1** · 1935–today · Fewer, bigger farms. The number of US farms peaked at about 6.8 million in 1935 and is now about 1.9 million, on larger acreages with fewer workers. Towns that served many small farms lost customers, rail traffic and young families as the farms consolidated.
  - Types: historical, economic. Source: USDA Census of Agriculture; USDA ERS farm counts.

## On Main Street, Dunmore itself

**Economic** (changes over years)

- **EC1** · 2019 · The park is sold to an investor. The family that owned Prairie View sold it to an out-of-state investment firm in 2019. Lot rent has gone up four times since. Residents own their homes but not the land, and moving a home costs more than it is worth.
  - Types: economic.
- **EC2** · 2016 · The last bank branch closes. The last branch closed in 2016. The two ATMs in town belong to other networks and charge $3 to $5 a withdrawal, and many older residents still pay with cash.
  - Types: economic.
- **EC3** · 2014 · Dollar stores replace the grocery. The independent grocery closed in 2014, a year after the second dollar store opened. Fresh food now means a 19-mile drive, so most shopping is canned and packaged food from the dollar store.
  - Types: economic.

**Political** (changes over decades)

- **P1** · state program · The state pays Medicare premiums for low incomes. For older residents with low incomes, the state pays the Medicare Part B premium, about $200 a month. Enrollment takes paperwork that many eligible people never finish.
  - Types: political.
- **P2** · state rates · Medicaid home care rates. Medicaid pays home-care agencies about $19 an hour. Aides earn far less, with no pay for the 35-mile drive between clients, so visits are short and often cancelled.
  - Types: political, economic.

**Built & natural** (changes over generations)

- **E1** · today · Thirty-five miles to the hospital. The nearest hospital and specialists are in Medianville, 35 miles on a two-lane highway. A routine appointment takes most of a day and someone to drive.
  - Types: environmental.

**Social & cultural** (changes over generations)

- **S1** · today · Aging in place. Most young adults left for Medianville or farther. Older residents stay in their homes, and care comes from a spouse, a neighbor, a church member or a relative who drives in.
  - Types: social, cultural. Rests on: H1, The railroad is abandoned.

**Historical** (bedrock, lasts a century)

- **H1** · 1979 · The railroad is abandoned. Dunmore grew up around a rail siding and a grain elevator. The railroad abandoned the branch in 1979, the elevator went to trucks, and Main Street lost the trade that came with the trains.
  - Types: historical, economic. Rests on: DH1, Fewer, bigger farms.

## Patterns: the records the block's circumstances shape

A record from the block's households that matches a pattern (the first that matches, in this order; the rules are regular expressions) carries its id in `block_pattern` and the circumstances it links to in `context_ids`. Pattern ids and loop ids are separate: pattern R1 is not loop R1.

- **N1** Lot rent (bill): links EC1; tagged when job_category matches `lot_rent`.
- **N2** ATM fees (bill): links EC2; tagged when fee_type matches `out_of_network_atm`.
- **N3** Dollar store groceries (purchase): links EC3; tagged when job_category matches `^food\.dollar_store$`.
- **N4** Medicare help from the state (income): links P1; tagged when job_category matches `medicare_part_b_state_buy_in`.
- **N5** Home-care visits (unpaid): links P2, S1; tagged when job_category matches `personal_care_aide_visit|home_health_nurse_visit`.
- **N6** Care from neighbors and kin (unpaid): links S1, E1; tagged when job_category matches `caregiving_visit|escort_to_appointment`.
- **N7** Car repairs (bill): links E1; tagged when job_category matches `car_repair|car_wont_start|jump_start|tow_and_roadside`.

## Loops (hypotheses for the next run to test)

- **R1 Lot-rent squeeze** (reinforcing). Each lot-rent increase leaves less cash. With less cash, moving the home out of the park is out of reach, so the owner can keep raising the rent.
  - Rent increases → Cash left after rent (−): More increases leave less cash.
  - Cash left after rent → Able to move out (+): More cash makes moving possible.
  - Able to move out → Rent increases (−): Fewer able to leave means increases stick.
  - Pushed + by EC1: An investor owner prices to what residents cannot escape.
  - Seen in the records of pattern N1.
- **B1 Neighbor care** (balancing). When an older neighbor needs care, others step in to visit and drive. Their help shrinks the unmet need, which holds the load in balance, until the helpers age too.
  - Care needed → Neighbors and kin help (+): More need brings more help.
  - Neighbors and kin help → Unmet care (−): More help leaves less unmet care.
  - Unmet care → Care needed (+): Unmet care turns into more need.
  - Pushed − by P2: Short, cancelled aide visits leave more to neighbors.
  - Seen in the records of pattern N6.
- **D1 The care gap** (reinforcing). When no aide comes, a family member covers the shift and loses work hours. The lost pay leaves less money for paid care, so more of the next week's shifts go unfilled too.
  - Aide shifts unfilled → Family member covers (+): More unfilled shifts mean more care from family.
  - Family member covers → Family work hours lost (+): More covering means more work hours lost.
  - Family work hours lost → Money for paid care (−): Lost hours leave less money for paid care.
  - Money for paid care → Aide shifts unfilled (−): Less money for paid care leaves more shifts unfilled.
  - Pushed + by DW2: Approved hours often have no aide to fill them.
  - Pushed + by DH1: Fewer working-age people stayed, so fewer are left to staff care.
  - Seen in the records of patterns N5, N6.

<!-- https://medianville.netlify.app/agents/districts/crossroads.md -->

# D6 Open country: Route 9 Crossroads

**Composite**: an invented block drawn from documented US patterns, not a real place. Part of https://medianville.netlify.app/agents/districts.md, which explains the layers and the ids.

Block id `crossroads`, on County Rd 12. Farm country consolidated in the 1980s, eleven miles from town, with no bus, no pharmacy and broadband that stops at Route 9.

The simulator puts 360 of the district's households on this block (`block_id = crossroads` in households.csv and records.csv).

## Across the whole district (the district tier)

**Economic** (changes over years)

- **DW2** · 2022 · Prices at the counter, debt after. When a prescription costs more than $250 out of pocket, more than half are left at the counter. 41% of adults carry health care debt, and about two-thirds of them have put off care because of cost.
  - Types: economic. Rests on: DW1, A pharmacy desert. Evidence: E058, E059, E060.

**Political** (changes over decades)

- **DW4** · 2025 · Seasonal guest workers. Farms here hire seasonal crews on H-2A visas, whose minimum wage is set by federal rule and has been fought over in court. Nationally they are a small group, but in farm counties they are much of the harvest.
  - Types: political, economic. Evidence: E087, E088.

**Built & natural** (changes over generations)

- **DW1** · 2024 · A pharmacy desert. Across open country, prescriptions mean a long drive. About 1 in 7 Americans lives in a pharmacy desert, and nonmetro residents average an 85-minute, 36-mile round trip. More than 7,000 pharmacies closed from 2022 through 2024.
  - Types: environmental, economic. Rests on: DE1, Services consolidated far away. Evidence: E056, E057.
- **DE1** · 1940–today · Services consolidated far away. Rural services were merged into fewer, farther places. The number of public school districts fell from about 117,000 in 1940 to about 13,000 today, and more than a hundred rural hospitals have closed or stopped inpatient care since 2010. Each merger added miles to ordinary trips.
  - Types: environmental, political. Rests on: DH1, The farm crisis. Source: NCES Digest of Education Statistics, table 214.10; UNC Sheps Center rural hospital closures.

**Social & cultural** (changes over generations)

- **DW3** · 2024 · Caregivers on the road. Out here a treatment day can be a whole day. In one rural region, dialysis patients ride a medical transit bus more than 200 miles, three days a week, and the family members who go with them say it takes most of their free time.
  - Types: social, economic. Rests on: DE1, Services consolidated far away. Evidence: E050.

**Historical** (bedrock, lasts a century)

- **DH1** · 1980s · The farm crisis. In the early 1980s high interest rates and falling export prices collapsed farmland values. From their 1982 peak to 1987 they fell by about a third nationally, and by more than half in Iowa. Many indebted farms were sold, and the people and businesses around them left too.
  - Types: historical, economic. Source: USDA ERS farm real estate values, as reported in FDIC, History of the Eighties, vol. 1, ch. 8 (1997).

## On Route 9 Crossroads itself

**Economic** (changes over years)

- **EC1** · today · Patchwork work. Year-round jobs are 11 miles away. Many households here piece together seasonal work at the packing shed, small self-employed jobs and gig work, paid irregularly and often through apps.
  - Types: economic. Rests on: H1, The farm crisis.
- **EC2** · 2018 · The pharmacy closes. The pharmacy at the crossroads closed in 2018 when its owner retired and no buyer came forward. Prescriptions come by mail now, a few days late when the mail is.
  - Types: economic.

**Political** (changes over decades)

- **P1** · today · No public transit in the county. The county has no bus. A volunteer van runs to Medianville once a week by reservation for medical trips. Anyone without a car pays a neighbor for rides to work.
  - Types: political.
- **P2** · 2009 · School districts consolidated. The township schools merged into a county district in 2009. Children ride the bus 50 minutes each way, and the district serves breakfast to everyone because so many leave home before 6:30.
  - Types: political.

**Built & natural** (changes over generations)

- **E1** · today · Broadband stops at Route 9. The cable line follows Route 9 and stops. East of the highway, internet means a phone plan, which works for deposits and payments but not much else.
  - Types: environmental, political.
- **E2** · today · Eleven miles to town. The nearest town is 11 miles away and the nearest city 25. Every errand, shift and appointment starts with a drive.
  - Types: environmental.

**Social & cultural** (changes over generations)

- **S1** · today · Church ride lists. The church at the crossroads keeps a list of who can drive when. Rides to work are paid, a few dollars toward gas; rides to the doctor usually are not.
  - Types: social, cultural.

**Historical** (bedrock, lasts a century)

- **H1** · 1980–95 · The farm crisis. High interest rates and falling land prices in the 1980s broke many family farms. Neighbors bought them out, and today four operations farm what forty families did. Former farm families stayed on and found other work.
  - Types: historical, economic. Rests on: DH1, The farm crisis.

## Patterns: the records the block's circumstances shape

A record from the block's households that matches a pattern (the first that matches, in this order; the rules are regular expressions) carries its id in `block_pattern` and the circumstances it links to in `context_ids`. Pattern ids and loop ids are separate: pattern R1 is not loop R1.

- **C1** Paid rides to work (bill): links P1, E2; tagged when job_category matches `ride_to_work_fee`.
- **C2** Self-employed and seasonal pay (income): links EC1, H1; tagged when job_category matches `self_employment_receipts|self_employed_supplies`.
- **C3** Prescriptions by mail (purchase): links EC2; tagged when job_category matches `prescription_mail_order`.
- **C4** Instant cash-outs (income): links EC1, E1; tagged when job_category matches `p2p_instant_cash_out|gig_payout_instant`.
- **C5** Deposits by phone (income): links E1; tagged when job_category matches `mobile_check_deposit`.
- **C6** School breakfast (unpaid): links P2; tagged when job_category matches `school_breakfast`.
- **C7** Care from neighbors (unpaid): links S1, E2; tagged when job_category matches `caregiving_visit|escort_to_appointment`.

## Loops (hypotheses for the next run to test)

- **R1 Ride debt** (reinforcing). Without a working car, getting to work means paying for rides. What goes to rides doesn't go to repairs, so the car stays broken and the rides continue.
  - A working car → Paid rides (−): No car means more paid rides.
  - Paid rides → Money for repairs (−): More paid rides leave less for repairs.
  - Money for repairs → A working car (+): Money for repairs keeps the car running.
  - Pushed + by P1: With no county transit, rides are the only option.
  - Seen in the records of pattern C1.
- **B1 Ride list** (balancing). When someone needs a ride, the church list finds a driver. The more drivers on the list, the fewer trips go unmade.
  - Rides needed → Drivers on the list (+): More need recruits more drivers.
  - Drivers on the list → Trips not made (−): More drivers mean fewer trips missed.
  - Trips not made → Rides needed (+): Missed trips come back as more need.
  - Pushed + by E2: Eleven miles to town makes every trip a ride.
  - Seen in the records of pattern C7.
- **D1 Distance and price** (reinforcing). Out here a prescription means a long drive, so some get skipped or put off. Conditions worsen, which means more trips to care, and every trip pays the distance again.
  - Miles to the pharmacy → Prescriptions skipped or delayed (+): More miles mean more prescriptions skipped or put off.
  - Prescriptions skipped or delayed → Condition worsens (+): Skipped doses let a condition worsen.
  - Condition worsens → More trips to care (+): A worse condition means more trips to care.
  - More trips to care → Miles to the pharmacy (+): More trips make the distance cost more.
  - Pushed + by DW1: A pharmacy desert puts the counter a long drive away.
  - Pushed + by DW2: Prices over $250 mean most are left at the counter.
  - Pushed + by DE1: Each consolidation adds miles between people and care.
  - Seen in the records of patterns C3, C7.

A payment here follows the Federal Reserve diary's idea: a purchase, bill or person-to-person payment made by an adult, by any instrument including EBT. It leaves out payroll deductions, credit-card bill payments (the purchases were already counted), ATM withdrawals and transfers between a person's own accounts.

Housing is the largest category, followed by transportation and food, as in the survey. A single day cannot match annual shares exactly: rent and mortgages bunch in the first days of the month, only about one worker in twenty is paid on a Wednesday the 3rd (so payroll-deducted Social Security and retirement contributions run low), and vehicle purchases are counted at full price on the day of sale. Recurring obligations spread over a month come to about $3,778,226 a day.

## Things that went wrong

- 6,168 records are failed attempts or ended declined, abandoned, failed or rescheduled; 1,907 later records are linked retries.
- 12.3% of households had at least one failed attempt (poverty 25.9%, ALICE 13.6%, above ALICE 9.3%).
- Card or account declines for insufficient funds: 683; technical declines: 651; declines during the card-reader outage at one grocery store: 45; overdrafts: 149; bounced autopays: 117.
- Purchases given up because nothing would cover them: 534. Prescriptions left at the counter over price: 86. Renewals stopped by the state portal outage: 3. Contractor no-shows: 8. Trips to a closed licensing office: 4.

Monthly benefits that post on other days are not in today's transfers: SSI and VA compensation arrived March 1, and most Social Security is paid on the second to fourth Wednesdays. Today's Social Security goes to people paid on the 3rd: long-time beneficiaries, people who also get SSI, and people whose Medicare premium the state pays. public_services_context.csv gives the daily cost of the services that are not itemized (police, roads, water, and so on).

## Consistency checks

- Time: the busiest person has 19.6 hours of work plus in-person activity; 0 people exceed 24 hours. In-person activities are scheduled into each person's free time, so no one is in two places at once.
- Money: opening balance plus inflows minus outflows equals closing balance for all but 0 households (household_ledger.csv). 168 checking accounts end the day overdrawn.
- Every payroll record has linked withholding and FICA records; every Social Security deposit with a Medicare premium has a linked deduction; retries point to the attempt that failed.
